questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Domain Where All Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{x}{y},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}(x,y)=1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ is defined only when $xy>0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.
$$

- The function ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}$ is defined only when $y\ne 0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y\ne 0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,xy>0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=xy{e}^{x/y}?$

- ${f}_{x}(0,1)$is defined
- ${f}_{y}(1,0)$ is defined
- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(1,1)$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(\frac{1}{y}) \\  & =y{e}^{x/y}+x{e}^{x/y} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x/y}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}+xy{e}^{x/y}(-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =x{e}^{x/y}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}{e}^{x/y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,1)=0\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{0/1}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{x}$ is also defined at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1)=1\cdot {e}^{0/1}+0\cdot {e}^{0/1}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(1,0)$ into ${f}_{y}$, we get

$$
{f}_{y}(1,0)=1\cdot {e}^{1/0}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{0}\cdot {e}^{1/0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(1,1)$, where we have 

$$
f(1,1)=1\cdot 1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e,
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}+1\cdot {e}^{1/1}=2e \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =1\cdot {e}^{1/1}-\frac{{1}^{2}}{1}\cdot {e}^{1/1}=e-e=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+y-{x}^{2}}}$ and

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{(1+y-{x}^{2})^{3}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\frac{z}{2\sqrt{(1+y-{x}^{2})^{3}}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+y-{x}^{2}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y,z)$ on which all partial derivatives of $f$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+y-{x}^{2}}}$ is defined only when $1+y-{x}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of $f$ is 

$$
{D}_{f}={(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${f}_{x}=\frac{xz}{\sqrt{(1+y-{x}^{2})^{3}}}$ is defined only when $1+y-{x}^{2}>0.$ So, the domain of ${f}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{f}_{x}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${f}_{y}$ and ${f}_{z}$ are the same

$$
{D}_{{f}_{y}}={D}_{{f}_{z}}={(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $f$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{y}}\cap {D}_{{f}_{z}} & ={D}_{f}\cap {D}_{{f}_{x}} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1}\cap {(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1} \\  & ={(x,y,z)\,:\,{x}^{2}<y+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $g(x,y)=\sqrt{y}\,{e}^{x/y}$ and

$$
\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{{e}^{x/y}}{\sqrt{y}},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{(y-2x)\,{e}^{x/y}}{2\sqrt{{y}^{3}}},
$$

find the set of values $(x,y)$ where all partial derivatives of $g$ exist.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that $g(x,y)=\sqrt{y}\,{e}^{x/y}$ is defined only when $y>0.$ So, the domain of $g$ is 

$$
{D}_{g}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

As for the partial derivatives, we have the following.

- The function ${g}_{x}(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{x/y}}{\sqrt{y}}$ is defined only when $y>0.$ So, the domain of ${g}_{x}$ is 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{x}}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

- Similarly, the domain of ${g}_{y}(x,y)$ is the same: 

$$
{D}_{{g}_{y}}={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.
$$

Finally, we conclude that the partials of $g$ exist on the set

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{g}\cap {D}_{{g}_{x}}\cap {D}_{{g}_{y}} & ={(x,y)\,:\,y\ge 0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y>0}\cap {(x,y)\,:\,y>0} \\  & ={(x,y)\,:\,y>0}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points Where Partial Derivatives Exist
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true about the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}?$

- Both partial derivatives exist at the point $(4,2)$
- ${f}_{x}(0,2)$ is defined
- ${f}_{y}(0,2)$ is defined
questions.worked_solution:
First, we compute the partial derivatives of $f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2{y}^{2}\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{2}{{y}^{3}}) \\  & =-\frac{2\sqrt{x}}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's examine the statements one-by-one.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the function $f$ is defined at $(4,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(4,2)=\frac{\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and both partial derivatives are also defined at $(4,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,2) & =\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{16} \\ {f}_{y}(4,2) & =-\frac{2\sqrt{4}}{{2}^{3}}=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If we substitute $(0,2)$ into ${f}_{x}$, we get

$$
{f}_{x}(0,2)=\frac{1}{2({2}^{2})\sqrt{0}}=\frac{1}{0},
$$

which is undefined since we have division by zero.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the function $f$ itself is defined at $(0,2)$, where we have 

$$
f(0,2)=\frac{\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{2}}=0,
$$

and ${f}_{y}$ is also defined at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(0,2)=-\frac{2\sqrt{0}}{{2}^{3}}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".
